title: How do you implement soft delete with EF Core global query filters?
description: HasQueryFilter for tenant/soft-delete rules, and the gotchas when includes and keys meet filters.

data.text: **Question:** How do you implement soft delete with EF Core global query filters?

Add a `DeletedAt`/`IsDeleted` marker to the entity, override `SaveChanges` so deletes write the marker instead of removing the row, and attach a **global query filter** (`builder.HasQueryFilter(e => !e.IsDeleted)`) so every query transparently excludes deleted records. The same mechanism handles multi-tenant scoping (`HasQueryFilter(e => e.TenantId == _tenantId)` with the tenant from a scoped service). Know the gotchas: filters don't compose with `Include` chains by default, unique indexes interact with soft deletes, and `Find`/tracked entities bypass assumptions.

**The pattern:**
- Base entity carries `IsDeleted` (bool) or `DeletedAt` (datetime?)
- `SaveChanges` override: for each entry marked `Deleted`, reset state to `Modified` and set the marker — the UPDATE persists it
- `HasQueryFilter(...)` in `OnModelCreating` hides marked rows from all queries of that entity type
- Global filters apply to **queries**, not to `ExecuteUpdate`/`ExecuteDelete` or raw SQL — those still see every row

**Gotchas a strong candidate lists:**
- **Filtered includes:** related collections are also filtered — `Include(b => b.Posts)` silently drops posts of a soft-deleted author's siblings... each level applies its own filter; there is no 'include everything' escape hatch (workaround: project or use `.IgnoreQueryFilters()` on a query you control)
- **Reference navigation to a filtered entity:** loading a `Post` whose `Author` is filtered gives `null` — surprising nulls in DTOs
- **Unique constraints:** `UNIQUE(Email)` still counts soft-deleted rows — re-registering the same email fails; use a filtered/partial unique index (`WHERE IsDeleted = 0`)
- **Keys and identity:** soft-deleted rows keep consuming keys; hard-delete is now a data operation, not an app operation
- **Duplicate filter definitions:** multiple filters on the same type AND together; EF warns when filter expressions differ between levels of a hierarchy (use an interface like `ISoftDeletable` consistently)
- **Tenancy + soft delete:** combine both in one filter; beware `IgnoreQueryFilters()` opening a tenant leak — audit every use
- **Find/track:** `Find` applies filters only when it queries; a tracked filtered-out entity can still be referenced

data.title: Soft delete with a SaveChanges override

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- The full mechanism (marker + SaveChanges override + HasQueryFilter), not just the filter
- Knowledge of what filters do **not** cover: includes, navigation nulls, raw SQL, unique indexes
- Multi-tenant awareness and the security angle of IgnoreQueryFilters
- Honest trade-offs: soft delete complicates indexes, keys, and compliance (hard purge)

items: Overriding Delete to set a flag but forgetting the query filter — nothing changes for readers
Assuming Include still returns related rows that are filtered out (silent nulls/empty lists)
UNIQUE constraints over soft-deleted rows blocking re-registration
Relying on filters in raw SQL or ExecuteUpdate — they are query-only
Ignoring filtered entities in reports that need true counts (COUNT must decide deleted-or-not explicitly)
Using IgnoreQueryFilters casually in multi-tenant queries — cross-tenant data exposure
How would you restore a soft-deleted entity along with its children?
How do global query filters behave in hierarchy/table-per-type mappings?
GDPR asks for real erasure — how does soft delete interact with that?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Marker + SaveChanges override + HasQueryFilter = transparent soft delete
Filters apply to queries only — includes, navigations, and raw SQL differ
Use filtered unique indexes so soft-deleted rows don't block re-use
Same mechanism powers tenant scoping — guard IgnoreQueryFilters
data.takeaway: Global query filters make 'deleted means hidden' the default — just remember every exception (includes, SQL, constraints) has to be designed for too.
